cards.front: Recall a key point about Key Sociological Perspectives
cards.back: Functionalism (Durkheim, Parsons): society is a system of interdependent parts working together to maintain stability. Each institution has a function: family socialises children, education teaches skills, economy provides material needs. Society is based on value consensus (shared norms and values).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Key Sociological Perspectives
cards.back: Marxism (Marx, Engels): society is divided by class conflict between the bourgeoisie (owners of production) and proletariat (workers). The ruling class controls the economy and ideology (institutions like education and media maintain ruling class dominance). Capitalism exploits workers and creates false consciousness (workers accept a system that exploits them).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Key Sociological Perspectives
cards.back: Feminism (Oakley, Barrett): society is patriarchal (male-dominated). Liberal feminism seeks reform through legislation. Marxist feminism sees patriarchy and capitalism as intertwined. Radical feminism sees patriarchy as the primary form of oppression, present in all institutions. Difference feminism recognises different women experience oppression differently.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Key Sociological Perspectives
cards.back: Interactionism (Becker, Goffman): society is created through everyday social interactions and meanings. Labelling theory: people are labelled and act according to those labels (Becker: 'deviance is not a quality of the act but of the response of others'). Goffman's dramaturgical model: social life is like a performance on a stage.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Key Sociological Perspectives
cards.back: Postmodernism (Lyotard, Baudrillard): there is no single truth or grand narrative. Society is diverse, fragmented and constantly changing. Media and technology create hyperreality (simulations that replace reality). Traditional perspectives are outdated because society has changed beyond what they can explain.

cards.front: What should you know about sociology exam tips?
cards.back: When comparing perspectives, always: identify what they agree/disagree about, use specific thinkers and concepts, evaluate using evidence, and consider whether perspectives complement or contradict each other.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Functionalism is no longer relevant because it cannot explain conflict and change in modern society.
